Usually an expression for one of these periods of time is more generalized in usage, and therefore it is probably satisfactory to adopt such an expression for any transition from darkness to light.

s.d: (the diminutive of ἔριφος but without special diminutive meaning{N:001}) kid, he-goat in the singular and goats in the plural (in the plural form both male and female goats are included in the reference)
s.c: Since goats are so widely distributed throughout the world, there is usually little or no difficulty involved in finding a satisfactory term. The difficulty arises, however, in the connotations of the term for goat, especially in contrast with sheep. In contrast with usage in the Bible, in many parts of the tropical world goats are much more highly prized than sheep, because they can forage well for themselves and are appreciated for their meat. Sheep, on the other hand, are often regarded as scavengers and are much less valued. One should not reverse biblical statements about sheep and goats, but marginal notes and a fuller explanation of cultural differences in a glossary are important.

general word for reptile that includes snakes and lizards
s.c: Though ἑρπετόν is often interpreted as referring only to snakes, it also includes in biblical contexts (as the result of the influence of classifications based on Hebrew terminology, as in ⟦Genesis 1:25|Genesis 1:25⟧, ⟦Genesis 1:26|Genesis 1:26⟧, ⟦Genesis 1:30|Genesis 1:30⟧ a number of small four-footed animals as well as snakes, for example, rats, mice, frogs, toads, salamanders, and lizards. However, in the various NT contexts (for example ⟦Acts 10:12|Acts 10:12⟧, ⟦Acts 11:6|Acts 11:6⟧, ⟦Romans 1:23|Romans 1:23⟧, ⟦James 3:7|James 3:7⟧ where ‘creeping things’ are contrasted with birds, animals, and fish) it is probably more satisfactory to use a term which designates primarily snakes. In a number of languages a very important distinction is made between four-footed reptiles (such as lizards) and snakes. If such a distinction is made, it is then probably better to use a term which designates only snakes, since a term for ‘animals’ will probably also include lizards.

In a number of languages it may be necessary to use a term in ⟦Hebrews 11:29|Hebrews 11:29⟧ which means ‘reddish,’ since an expression meaning ‘bright red’ might seem entirely inappropriate in speaking of a body of water.

s.d: (an idiom, literally: the inner (person)) the psychological faculty, including intellectual, emotional, and spiritual aspects, in contrast with the purely physical aspects of human existence
s.g: the inner being; the inmost being; inwardly
s.c: In a number of languages it is quite impossible to speak of the psychological faculty of a person as being merely ‘that which is within.’ It is frequently necessary to refer to a particular organ of the body, for example, ‘the heart’ or ‘the liver’ or ‘the spleen.’ In some languages, however, one may refer to this faculty as being ‘the person who stands inside’ or ‘the real person’ or even ‘the other person.’|In ⟦Luke 17:21|Luke 17:21⟧ the phrase ἐντὸς ὑμῶν in the statement ἰδοὺ γὰρ ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ἐντὸς ὑμῶν ἐστιν ‘look, God’s reign is within you’ may constitute a reference to the same inner being designated by the phrases ὁ ἔσω and ὁ ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ. On this basis some scholars have suggested that the phrase ἐντὸς ὑμῶν can be interpreted as a potentiality for participation and hence be translated ‘within your grasp,’ but it is more likely that one should understand the phrase ἐντὸς ὑμῶν in ⟦Luke 17:21|Luke 17:21⟧ as a spacial relationship, for example, ‘in your midst’ or ‘among you’ (see LN 83.9).

s.dp: Spacial Extensions › Extension From a Source
s.d: extension from a source which is inside

s.dp: Spacial Positions › Among, Between, In, Inside
s.d: the inner surface of an object
(a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ἔσωθεν<SDBG:ἔσωθεν:000000>}[a] ‘from inside,’ {D:84.14}) the inner being of a person as the source or agent of thought or behavior
s.g: a person’s inner self; the inner being; within oneself
s.c: A literal translation of ἔσωθεν δέ εἰσιν λύκοι ἅρπαγες in ⟦Matthew 7:15|Matthew 7:15⟧ as ‘on the inside they are ravaging wolves’ could be seriously misleading, since in some cultures certain people are regarded as actually being animals but disguised as human beings. It may therefore be necessary to make some adjustments in this passage and to translate as ‘but what they want to do makes them like wild wolves’ or ‘but their minds are like the minds of wild wolves.’ On the other hand, one could employ a strictly literal translation and then have a footnote indicating that this statement in the Scriptures does not confirm local beliefs concerning animals disguised as humans.

s.dp: Spacial Positions › Among, Between, In, Inside
s.d: pertaining to a position within an area
a person who is associated with someone else, though not necessarily involving personal affection (as in the case of {L:φίλος<SDBG:φίλος:000000>} and φίλη, {D:34.11} and {D:34.12})
s.c: This meaning is also found as a variant reading: ὁμοία ἐστὶν παιδίοις καθημένοις ἐν ταῖς ἀγοραῖς ἅ προσφωνοῦντα τοῖς ἑταίροις ‘like children sitting around in the marketplace and shouting to their companions’ ⟦Matthew 11:16|Matthew 11:16⟧ (apparatus; see Nestle-Aland).

s.d: pertaining to being a different or strange language
s.g: speaking in a strange language; in a strange language

s.d: teach that which is different from what should be taught
s.g: to teach a different doctrine; to teach something different
s.c: In rendering ἑτεροδιδασκαλέω in ⟦1 Timothy 1:3|1 Timothy 1:3⟧, it may be necessary to be specific about the particular doctrine which forms the basis of contrast, for example, ‘that you may order them to stop teaching a doctrine which is different from what has already been taught’ or ‘… from what I have already taught’ or ‘… from what they ought to teach.’

s.d: to be wrongly or poorly matched in an association
s.g: to be mismatched; to be wrongly matched
s.c: It is often necessary to indicate somewhat more precisely the manner in which one may be wrongly matched with others. Accordingly, one can translate ⟦2 Corinthians 6:14|2 Corinthians 6:14⟧ as ‘do not attempt to work together with those who are unbelievers’ or ‘do not become partners with those who do not believe.’

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Different Kind or Class
s.d: pertaining to that which is different in kind or class from all other entities{N:001}

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Different Kind or Class
s.d: pertaining to that which is other than some other item implied or identified in a context{N:001}

s.dp: Time › Units of Time with Reference to Other Units or Points of Time: Yesterday, Today, Next Day
s.d: a day immediately following a previous day{N:002}
s.g: the next day; on the next day

s.d: a marker of something in addition to what is already implied in the context

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Different Kind or Class
s.d: pertaining to that which is different in kind or class from all other entities{N:001}

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
s.d: extension of time up to and beyond an expected point
the state of something being in addition to what already exists
s.c: The sequence ἔτι τε καί in ⟦Luke 14:26|Luke 14:26⟧ is clearly emphatic, so that one might well render the expression ἔτι τε καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν ἑαυτοῦ as ‘and he himself as well.’

s.d: a marker of contrast, involving something contrary to expectation
(derivative of {L:ἑτοιμασία<SDBG:ἑτοιμασία:000000>} ‘readiness,’ {D:77.1}) to cause to be ready
a state of being ready for action
pertaining to a state of readiness
pertaining to a state of readiness

s.dp: Time › Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
s.d: a unit of time involving a complete cycle of seasons
s.c: In a number of languages, years are described in terms of repeated seasons. For example, some languages would speak of ‘twelve years’ as being ‘twelve winters’ or ‘twelve summers,’ while in other languages one might have an expression such as ‘twelve rainy seasons’ or ‘twelve returns of the sun.’

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: possibly a symbolic temporal expression denoting a very long period of time
s.c: Though most translations render ἔτη τεσσεράκοντα as ‘forty years,’ the expression probably is to be understood as meaning an unusually long period of time. See also discussion at LN 67.93.

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: (an idiom, literally: through years) a point of time subsequent to another point of time after an interval of some years

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Goodness
s.d: that which is good in the sense of beneficial
pertaining to events which measure up to their intended purpose
s.g: fine; well; good; excellent; well done
s.c: In the LN 65.23 contexts, βελτίων, καλῶς, εὖ, and εὖγε occur in highly elliptical constructions.

s.d: pertaining to events which measure up to their intended purpose
s.g: fine; well; good; excellent; well done
s.c: In the LN 65.23 contexts, βελτίων, καλῶς, εὖ, and εὖγε occur in highly elliptical constructions.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: ancestor of the human race
to communicate good news concerning something (in the NT a particular reference to the gospel message about Jesus)
s.g: to tell the good news; to announce the gospel
s.c: In ⟦Luke 1:19|Luke 1:19⟧, however, the reference is to the birth of John the Baptist.

s.d: (derivative of {L:εὐαγγελίζω<SDBG:εὐαγγελίζω:000000>} ‘to tell the good news,’ {D:33.215}) the content of good news (in the NT a reference to the gospel about Jesus)
s.c: In a number of languages the expression ‘the gospel’ or ‘the good news’ must be rendered by a phrase, for example, ‘news that makes one happy’ or ‘information that causes one joy’ or ‘words that bring smiles’ or ‘a message that causes the heart to be sweet.’

s.d: one who announces the gospel
s.c: Though the term εὐαγγελιστής indicates only an individual who ‘announces the gospel,’ early usage would suggest that this was often a person who went from place to place announcing the good news.
